Analysis by Richard Cowan

Recently, an article in the Montreal (French) daily La Presse reported that a survey by

Health Canada found **“some” Canadian doctors now support “the use of cannabis when all

other conventional treatments have failed.”**

Isn’t that special? “When all other conventional treatments have failed…” This

precondition means that patients will have to suffer greatly before their doctors—and in

Canada, it is very difficult to change doctors—will consider the medical use of cannabis,

even though there are numerous conditions for which there are really no effective

conventional treatments.

For example, there are now ads on television (in the U.S., but seen on Canadian cable) for a

new drug called Lyrica, “for the management of fibromyalgia. It is also used to help people

with diabetes manage nerve pain and for pain after shingles.” The ads specifically say that

it is the first drug approved for fibromyalgia. The ad also goes on to list the rather scary-

sounding side effects.

From http://www.lyrica.com/content/main_safety_information.jsp

“Some of the most common side effects of LYRICA are dizziness, sleepiness, dry mouth, and

edema. Plus blurred vision, weight gain, constipation, euphoric mood, and loss of balance.

Also, increase appetite and trouble concentrating.

LYRICA may cause serious allergic reactions. You should call your doctor right away if you

think you have a serious allergic reaction such as swelling of the face, mouth, lips, gums,

tongue or neck or if you have any trouble breathing. Other allergic reactions may include

rash, hives and blisters.

You may have a higher chance for swelling and hives if you are also taking angiotensin

converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitors so you should let your doctor know if you are taking these

medications. You may have a higher chance of swelling or gaining weight if you are also

taking certain diabetes medicines. And, if you drink alcohol or take medicines that make you

sleepy, you may feel more sleepy when you start LYRICA.

You should not drive a car or work with machines until you know how LYRICA affects you.

Tell your doctor about any changes in your eyesight, muscle pain along with a fever or tired

feeling, or skin sores due to diabetes. Also tell your doctor if you are planning to father a

child. Tell your doctor if you are pregnant, plan to become pregnant, or are breast-feeding. If

you have had a drug or alcohol problem, you may be more likely to misuse LYRICA. You

should talk with your doctor before you stop taking LYRICA, or any other prescription

medication.”

Of course, cannabis is widely used by people with fibromyalgia and other forms of neuropathy (nerve pain), and they experience none of the more serious side effects but do sometimes experience a “euphoric mood”, which we are told is an intolerable consequence when it is caused by cannabis. And there is an “increased appetite”, AKA the munchies.

Amusingly, La Presse seems to have had to use the Canadian equivalent of the American Freedom of Information Act to find out about the December study, which is based on the testimonials of only 30 Canadian doctors.

The Canadian Medical Association has really tried to block the medical use of cannabis. Supposedly, they fear their members will be perceived as "pushers" and have always said they needed “more research”.

Incredibly, the Canadian government spent C$2 million from 2001-2006 on a study of cannabis for pain, but the Conservative government canceled the project in September 2006.

“about 2% of the population could claim

the right to use marijuana for medical reasons, based on self-identified needs…"

The point of all this is simply that we cannot give the quacks control over cannabis.
